questions.explanation: A vacuum flask's double-walled, evacuated design already blocks conduction and convection (no medium to carry heat) and its silvered walls minimise radiation. The airtight stopper's specific job is to stop the liquid's vapour from escaping, since evaporation carries away latent heat and would otherwise cool the contents rapidly. Students often default to "convection" since flasks are famous for blocking that, missing that the stopper's specific function targets evaporation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Friction] I. The frictional force is independent of the area of the surfaces in contact II. The frictional force depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact III. The frictional force depends on the speed of sliding IV. The frictional force is directly proportional to the normal reaction. Which combination of the above is true of sliding friction?
questions.explanation: The laws of sliding friction state that friction is independent of contact area (I), depends on the nature/roughness of the surfaces (II), and is proportional to the normal reaction force (IV) via F = μN. Statement III is false — kinetic friction is approximately independent of sliding speed for most surfaces, which is precisely the property that makes Coulomb's friction model useful. Watch for "independent of area" and "independent of speed" being swapped as a trap.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Simple Harmonic Motion / Pendulum] A simple pendulum has a period of 17.0s. When the length is shortened by 1.5m, its period is 8.5s. Calculate the original length of the pendulum
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), the ratio T₁/T₂ = √(L/(L−1.5)) = 17/8.5 = 2. Squaring gives 4 = L/(L−1.5), so 4L − 6 = L, and 3L = 6, giving L = 2.0m. The key technique is using the ratio of periods to eliminate g and 2π entirely rather than solving for g first — a common time-wasting trap under exam pressure.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Gas Discharge / Conduction in Gases] A gas would serve as an electrical conductor under
questions.explanation: Gases are normally insulators, but at reduced pressure, the mean free path of ions increases, letting them accelerate enough between collisions to ionise further gas molecules and sustain a discharge (as in fluorescent tubes and discharge tubes) — this requires reduced pressure paired with a sufficiently high potential/current to drive ionisation, not a reduced potential (which would fail to ionise the gas at all, ruling out option C).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Refraction / Apparent Depth] A boy observes a piece of stone at the bottom of a river 6.0m deep. If he looks from the surface of the river, what is the apparent distance of the stone from him? [Refractive Index of Water = 4/3]
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = real depth ÷ refractive index = 6.0 ÷ (4/3) = 4.5m. The stone appears closer than it really is because light bends away from the normal as it exits water into air, an effect exploited in the classic "why does a pool look shallower than it is" demonstration. The trap is multiplying instead of dividing by the refractive index, which produces option A (8.0m).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Simple Machines] The velocity ratio of a machine is 5 and its efficiency is 75%. What effort would be needed to lift a load of 150N with the machine?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = Mechanical Advantage ÷ Velocity Ratio, so MA = efficiency × VR = 0.75 × 5 = 3.75. Since MA = Load/Effort, Effort = Load/MA = 150/3.75 = 40N. A common trap is using VR directly as MA (ignoring the 75% efficiency loss), which would give 30N instead — always apply efficiency before dividing for effort in a non-ideal machine.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Fluids — Archimedes' Principle / Floatation] When a ship sails from salt water into fresh water, the fraction of its volume above the water surface will
questions.explanation: Fresh water is less dense than salt water, so by Archimedes' principle the ship must displace a greater volume of fresh water to generate the same upward buoyant force equal to its weight. This means the ship sinks lower, decreasing the fraction of its volume that remains above the surface. This is the same principle behind Plimsoll lines marked on ship hulls for different water types.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — AC Circuits / Inductive Reactance]
options: Supply. The reactance of the inductor is
questions.explanation: Inductive reactance is X_L = 2πfL. Substituting f = 50/π Hz and L = 2H: X_L = 2π × (50/π) × 2 = 200Ω — the π terms cancel neatly, which is exactly why the frequency was deliberately given in that unusual form. Spotting that the π in the formula cancels the π in the given frequency is the fast route to the answer; grinding through decimal π approximations wastes time.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Power Transmission and Power Loss] An electric generator with a power output of 3.0KW at a voltage of 1.5KV distributes power along cables of resistance 20.0Ω. The power loss in the cables is
questions.explanation: Current in the cable: I = P/V = 3000/1500 = 2A. Power loss in the cable resistance: P_loss = I²R = 2² × 20 = 80W. This is the core reason power is transmitted at high voltage/low current over long distances — halving current quarters the resistive loss. A common trap is using the transmission voltage (1.5kV) directly in P=V²/R instead of first finding the actual current flowing.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Solid State Physics — Semiconductors] In a pure semiconductor, the number of electrons in the conduction band is
options: less than the number of holes in the valence band
equal to the number of holes in the valence band
greater than the number of holes in the valence band
twice the number of holes in the valence band
questions.explanation: In an intrinsic (pure, undoped) semiconductor, every electron that is thermally excited into the conduction band leaves behind exactly one hole in the valence band. Electron-hole pairs are always created and destroyed together, so their populations stay equal at all times. This equality breaks down only in doped (extrinsic) semiconductors, where impurities deliberately create an excess of one carrier type.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Lenses / Magnification] A projection lantern is used to give the image of a slide on a screen. If the image is 24 times as large as the slide and the screen is 72.0m from the projecting lens, what is the position of the slide from the lens?
questions.explanation: Linear magnification m = v/u, where v is image distance and u is object (slide) distance. Given m = 24 and v = 72.0m, u = v/m = 72/24 = 3.0m. The trap here is multiplying instead of dividing (72 × 24), which would wildly overshoot any sensible slide-to-lens distance — always sanity-check that the object distance for magnified projection is smaller than the image distance, not larger.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Wave Equation] A travelling wave moving from left to right has an amplitude of 0.15m, a frequency of 550Hz and a wavelength of 0.01m. The equation describing the wave is
questions.explanation: The general wave equation is y = A sin[k(x − vt)], where k = 2π/λ = 2π/0.01 ≈ 200π rad/m and wave speed v = fλ = 550 × 0.01 = 5.5 m/s. Substituting gives y = 0.15 sin[200π(x − 5.5t)], matching option A exactly in both the wavenumber and the wave speed factored inside the bracket. The distractors scramble which numbers belong with x versus t, so always derive k and v independently before matching to the options.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Change of State] A thin wire with heavy weights attached to both ends is hung over a block of ice resting on two supports. If the wire cuts through the ice block while the block remains solid behind the wire, the process is called
questions.explanation: This is the classic regelation demonstration: pressure from the thin wire lowers the local melting point of ice, melting it just ahead of the wire; once the wire passes, the pressure is released and the water instantly refreezes behind it, leaving the ice block intact. Fusion (D) is simply melting under normal conditions and doesn't capture the pressure-dependent refreezing that defines regelation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Standing/Progressive Waves on Strings] One end of a long wire is fixed while a vibrator is attached to the other end. When the vibrator is energized, the types of waves generated in the wire are
questions.explanation: The vibrator produces transverse waves (particle motion perpendicular to the wire), which travel along the wire and reflect off the fixed end. The incident and reflected waves of the same frequency and amplitude superpose to form a stationary (standing) wave pattern with fixed nodes and antinodes. This is the working principle behind sonometer and Melde's experiment setups tested regularly in JAMB.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Photoelectric Effect] Light of energy 5eV falls on a metal of work function 3eV and electrons are liberated. The stopping potential is
questions.explanation: By Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons equals photon energy minus work function: KE_max = 5eV − 3eV = 2eV. Since the stopping potential (in volts) numerically equals the maximum kinetic energy (in eV) divided by the electron charge, the stopping potential is 2.0V. The trap is adding instead of subtracting the work function, which produces option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Optical Instruments] What optical instrument can best be constructed with converging lenses of focal lengths 50cm and 5cm?
questions.explanation: An astronomical (refracting) telescope uses two converging lenses: an objective of long focal length (50cm) and an eyepiece of short focal length (5cm), separated by the sum of their focal lengths for normal adjustment. A compound microscope also uses two converging lenses but both have short focal lengths for high magnification of nearby objects, which doesn't fit this 50cm/5cm pairing designed for distant objects.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Radioactive Decay / Half-life] If the fraction of the atoms of a radioactive material left after 120 years is 1/64, what is the half-life of the material?
questions.explanation: Since (1/2)ⁿ = 1/64 = (1/2)⁶, exactly 6 half-lives have elapsed in 120 years, giving a half-life of 120/6 = 20 years. The key skill is recognising 64 as 2⁶ quickly — students who instead try to solve using the decay constant formula directly often waste time or make sign errors under pressure.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Power, Work and Energy] If the force and the velocity on a system are each reduced simultaneously by half, the power of the system is
questions.explanation: Power P = Fv. If both F and v are halved, the new power is (F/2)(v/2) = Fv/4, i.e., a quarter of the original. This is a direct consequence of power depending on the product of two quantities — halving two multiplied factors always divides the product by four, not by two.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Anomalous Expansion of Water] A quantity of water at 0°C is heated to about 30°C. At each degree rise in temperature, its density will
questions.explanation: Water exhibits anomalous expansion: as it's heated from 0°C to 4°C, it actually contracts, so density rises to a maximum at 4°C; beyond 4°C, normal thermal expansion takes over and density falls steadily as temperature continues to rise toward 30°C. This anomaly (density rising then falling, not falling then rising) is why ice floats and why lakes freeze from the top down, protecting aquatic life below.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Reflection at Plane Mirrors] An engineer intends to deviate a light ray from its path by 120° through reflection from a plane mirror. Calculate the angle of incidence
questions.explanation: For reflection off a plane mirror, the deviation of the ray equals 180° − 2i, where i is the angle of incidence. Setting 180 − 2i = 120 gives 2i = 60, so i = 30°. A frequent trap is confusing the angle of incidence with the deviation angle itself, or halving 120° directly (giving 60°, option A) without accounting for the 180° relationship.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Circular Motion] I. Its velocity is constant II. No work is done on the body III. It has constant acceleration directed away from the centre IV. The centripetal force is directed towards the centre Which combination of the above is true of a body moving with constant speed in a circular track?
questions.explanation: For uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity is not (its direction constantly changes), so statement I is false. The centripetal force acts toward the centre (IV, true) and is always perpendicular to the velocity, meaning it does no work on the body (II, true). Statement III is false on two counts: the acceleration is centripetal (directed toward, not away from, the centre), ruling out any option pairing III with a correct answer.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Resolution of Forces / Vectors] A handbag containing some load weighing 162N is carried by two students each holding the handle of the bag next to him. If each handle is pulled 60° to the vertical, find the force on each student's arm
questions.explanation: The two tension forces, each at 60° to the vertical, must have their vertical components sum to support the full weight: 2T·cos(60°) = 162N. Since cos(60°) = 0.5, this simplifies to 2T(0.5) = T = 162N. The trap is assuming the load simply splits evenly between the two arms (giving 81N, option A), which ignores that the greater the angle from vertical, the more tension is needed per arm to support the same vertical load.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Current Electricity — Internal Resistance and Efficiency] A cell of internal resistance 1Ω supplies current to an external resistor of 3Ω. The efficiency of the cell is
questions.explanation: The efficiency of a cell is the fraction of total power delivered to the external (useful) resistance: efficiency = R/(R+r) = 3/(3+1) = 3/4 = 75%. This reflects that most of the e.m.f. is being used productively in the external circuit rather than wasted as heat inside the cell's own internal resistance. The trap is computing r/(R+r) instead, inverting the fraction to give 25% (option A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Wave Speed on a Stretched String] A transverse wave is applied to a string whose mass per unit length is 3 x 10⁻² kgm⁻¹. If the string is under a tension 12N, the speed of the propagation of the wave is
questions.explanation: Wave speed on a stretched string is given by v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length. Substituting: v = √(12/0.03) = √400 = 20 m/s. This formula shows why guitar and violin strings under higher tension produce faster wave propagation, and hence higher pitched notes for a given string length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Types of Radioactive Radiation] A certain radioactive source emits radiations that were found to be deflected by both magnetic and electric fields. The radiations are
questions.explanation: Beta particles are fast-moving electrons and therefore carry charge, so they are deflected by both magnetic and electric fields (though less than alpha particles due to their smaller mass, they deflect much further in the same field). Gamma rays and X-rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation and are unaffected by either type of field, which is precisely how scientists distinguish charged from uncharged radioactive emissions in a deflection experiment.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Humidity / Hygrometry] Dry Day 1 - 30°C | Day 2 - 29°C | Day 3 - 25°C Wet Day 1 - 22°C | Day 2 - 22°C | Day 3 - 21°C The readings above are for three consecutive days from a wet and dry bulb hygrometer. It can be concluded that the relative humidity for the three days
questions.explanation: The depression (dry-bulb minus wet-bulb reading) shrinks steadily across the three days: 8°C, 7°C, then 4°C. A smaller depression means less evaporative cooling is occurring at the wet bulb, which happens when the surrounding air is already closer to saturation — so a shrinking depression signals rising relative humidity. Since the depression is largest on Day 1, humidity was in fact lowest (not least, i.e., ruling out D) that day, and it increased steadily afterward.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Relative Velocity] A stream is flowing at 0.75ms⁻¹ and a boat heading perpendicular for the stream landed at the opposite bank at an angle of 30° to the direct crossing path. Calculate the velocity of the boat.
questions.explanation: The stream's velocity is the component of the resultant velocity along the bank, related to the resultant by sin(30°) = v_stream/v_resultant. Solving: v_resultant = 0.75/sin(30°) = 0.75/0.5 = 1.50 m/s. The 30° drift angle tells us how far off-course the current pushed the boat relative to its straight-across heading, which lets us reconstruct the full resultant velocity using basic trigonometry on the velocity triangle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor] A conductor of length 2m carries a current of 0.8A while kept in a magnetic field of magnetic flux density 0.5T. The maximum force acting on it is
questions.explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is F = BIL, maximised when the conductor is perpendicular to the field. Substituting: F = 0.5 × 0.8 × 2 = 0.8N. This is the fundamental equation underlying how electric motors and moving-coil galvanometers generate mechanical force from electric current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Kinematics / Calculus of Motion] The velocity y of a particle in a time t is given by the equation y = 10 + 2t². Find the instantaneous acceleration after 5 seconds
questions.explanation: Since y here represents velocity, instantaneous acceleration is the derivative dy/dt = 4t. At t = 5s, acceleration = 4 × 5 = 20 m/s². The trap is treating y as displacement and differentiating twice, or substituting t=5 into y itself instead of into its derivative — always confirm what physical quantity the given equation represents before differentiating.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Newton's Second Law / Tension] A rope is being used to pull a mass of 10kg vertically upward. Determine the tension in the rope if, starting from rest, the mass acquires a velocity of 4ms⁻¹ in 8s [g = 10ms⁻²]
questions.explanation: First find acceleration: a = (v−u)/t = 4/8 = 0.5 m/s². Applying Newton's second law to a mass being lifted, the rope must overcome gravity and provide the net upward acceleration: T − mg = ma, so T = m(g+a) = 10 × (10+0.5) = 105N. The trap is calculating only the net force (ma = 5N, option A) and forgetting the rope must also support the object's full weight against gravity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Motion of Charges in Combined Fields] If a charged ion goes through combined electric and magnetic fields, the resultant emergent velocity of the ion is
questions.explanation: This describes a velocity selector: when the electric force (qE) and magnetic force (qvB) on the charged ion are balanced and opposite, the ion passes straight through undeflected. Setting qE = qvB and solving gives v = E/B. This principle is used in mass spectrometers to select ions of a specific velocity before further analysis, filtering out ions travelling at any other speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Curved Mirrors] The driving mirror of a car has a radius of curvature of 1m. A vehicle behind the car is 4m from the mirror. Find the image distance behind the mirror.
questions.explanation: > A driving (rear-view) mirror is convex, with focal length f = R/2 = 0.5m (virtual, behind the mirror). Using the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with the real-is-positive sign convention (f = −0.5m, u = −4m), solving gives v = −4/7m, meaning the image forms 4/7m behind the mirror. Convex mirrors always form a virtual, diminished image behind the mirror regardless of object distance — this is exactly why they give drivers a wider field of view.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electrostatics — Capacitors and Dielectrics] When a piece of rectangular glass block is inserted between two parallel capacitor plates, at constant plate area and distance of separation, the capacitance of the capacitor will
questions.explanation: > Inserting a dielectric like glass between capacitor plates increases capacitance because C = εᵣε₀A/d, and glass has a relative permittivity (dielectric constant) εᵣ greater than 1 (the value for air/vacuum). The dielectric material polarises in the electric field, weakening the net field between the plates and allowing more charge to be stored for the same voltage.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Vector Addition of Forces] The resultant of two forces acting on an object is maximum if the angle between them is
questions.explanation: > The resultant of two forces is given by R = √(F₁² + F₂² + 2F₁F₂cosθ), which is maximised when cosθ = 1, i.e., when θ = 0° and both forces point in exactly the same direction, so their magnitudes add directly. At 180° (opposite directions), the resultant would instead be at its minimum, which is the trap many students confuse with the maximum case.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Fluids — Archimedes' Principle / Volume Displacement] If a spherical metal bob of radius 3cm is fully immersed in a cylinder containing water and the water level rises by 1cm, what is the radius of the cylinder?
questions.explanation: > The volume of water displaced equals the sphere's volume: (4/3)πr³ = πR²h, where r = 3cm is the sphere's radius and h = 1cm is the rise in water level. Solving: R² = (4/3)(3)³/1 = 36, so R = 6cm. This is a classic application of displacement volume used to indirectly measure irregular solid volumes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Heat Transfer Mechanisms] Ice cubes are added to a glass of warm water. The glass and water are cooled by
questions.explanation: > Heat transfers directly from the water to the ice cubes by conduction at the points of contact, while convection currents circulate the cooler water (denser, so it sinks) throughout the glass, spreading the cooling effect. Radiation plays a negligible role here since it typically matters only for very hot objects or across a vacuum, not for cooling by direct contact with ice in liquid water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Magnetic Force on Moving Charges] The magnetic force on a charged particle moving with velocity v is
options: proportional to both the magnitude of the charge and the velocity v
independent of the magnitude of the charge
proportional to the velocity v only
proportional to the magnitude of the charge only
questions.explanation: > The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by F = qvB sinθ, showing direct proportionality to both the charge's magnitude (q) and its velocity (v). A particle with zero charge or zero velocity experiences no magnetic force at all, confirming that both factors must be present simultaneously — neither one alone (options C or D) captures the full dependency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Telescopes] The terrestrial telescope has one extra lens more than the astronomical telescope. The extra lens is for
questions.explanation: > An astronomical telescope produces an inverted final image, which is acceptable for viewing celestial objects but impractical for viewing objects on Earth. The terrestrial telescope adds a third "erecting lens" specifically to invert the image back to upright, without adding any extra magnification — the erecting lens contributes nothing to magnification power, only orientation correction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Solid State Physics — Transistors] A transistor functions mainly as a
questions.explanation: > A transistor's two primary applications are as an electronic switch (turning current on/off, the basis of digital logic) and as an amplifier (boosting weak signals using a small base current to control a much larger collector current). Rectification is instead the job of diodes, and charge storage is the function of capacitors, not transistors — both distractors borrow functions from other components.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics/Fluids — Atmospheric Pressure with Altitude] The height at which the atmosphere ceases to exist is about 80km. If the atmospheric pressure on the ground level is 760mmHg, the pressure at a height of 20km above the ground level is
questions.explanation: > Treating the pressure decrease as linear with height (the simplification JAMB expects at this level): pressure remaining = 760 × (1 − 20/80) = 760 × 0.75 = 570mmHg. The trap is assuming pressure halves at the midpoint of altitude (as with exponential atmospheric models), which would give 380mmHg — JAMB's simplified linear model is what's tested here, not the true exponential barometric formula.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Scalars and Vectors] Which of the following consists entirely of vector quantities?
questions.explanation: > Velocity, displacement, and reaction (a contact force) are all vector quantities, having both magnitude and direction. The distractors each smuggle in one scalar: mass (option B) and power (option C) are scalars, while work and pressure (option D) are also scalars — only moment (torque) in option D is a vector, making the whole set fail.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Conduction Through Gases] I. Low pressure. II. High pressure. III. High p.d. IV. Low p.d. Which combination of the above is true of the conduction of electricity through gases?
questions.explanation: > Gases conduct electricity effectively when at low pressure (I), since the increased mean free path lets ions accelerate to higher speeds between collisions, ionising more gas molecules, and typically requires a high potential difference (III) to initially strip electrons and sustain the discharge. High pressure suppresses ionisation by increasing collision frequency, which is why option combinations involving II are incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Work Done by a Gas] A gas with initial volume of 2 x 10⁻⁶m³ is allowed to expand to six times its initial value at constant pressure of 2 x 10⁵Nm⁻². The work done is?
questions.explanation: > For isobaric (constant pressure) expansion, work done = PΔV = P(V₂ − V₁). Here V₂ = 6 × 2×10⁻⁶ = 12×10⁻⁶m³, so ΔV = 10×10⁻⁶m³, giving W = 2×10⁵ × 10×10⁻⁶ = 2.0J. The trap is using the final volume directly instead of the change in volume, which inflates the answer well beyond the correct result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Transformers and Eddy Currents] Energy losses through eddy currents are reduced by using
questions.explanation: > Eddy currents are induced loops of current within a solid conducting core, and they're minimised by laminating the core into thin, mutually insulated soft iron sheets, which breaks up the large conducting loops that would otherwise sustain strong eddy currents. Soft iron is chosen specifically for its high magnetic permeability alongside the insulation, not for its resistance value per se — the insulation between laminations, not the wire's own resistance, is what suppresses the loops.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Thermometry] The thermometric substance of an absolute thermometer is
questions.explanation: > An absolute (constant-volume gas) thermometer uses a fixed volume of gas, typically helium, because it stays gaseous down to extremely low temperatures and behaves very close to an ideal gas over a wide range, making it the most reliable reference for defining the absolute (Kelvin) temperature scale. Mercury and alcohol thermometers, by contrast, rely on liquid expansion and cannot function anywhere near absolute zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Standing Waves / Harmonics] A string is fastened tightly between two walls 24cm apart. The wavelength of the second overtone is
questions.explanation: > For a string fixed at both ends, the nth harmonic has wavelength λₙ = 2L/n. The second overtone is the third harmonic (n=3), since the first overtone is the second harmonic. So λ₃ = 2(24)/3 = 16cm. The recurring trap in overtone questions is off-by-one errors — always remember "second overtone" means the third harmonic, not literally n=2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Cost of Electrical Energy] The cost of running five 60 W lamps and four 100 W lamps for 20 hours if electrical energy cost #10.00 per kwh is
questions.explanation: > Total power = (5×60) + (4×100) = 300 + 400 = 700W = 0.7kW. Energy used over 20 hours = 0.7 × 20 = 14kWh. At ₦10.00 per kWh, total cost = 14 × 10 = ₦140.00. This is a standard "energy cost" question format — always convert total wattage to kilowatts before multiplying by hours and unit cost.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Current Electricity — Cell Efficiency and Internal Resistance] A cell of internal resistance r supplies current to a 6.0Ω resistor and its efficiency is 75%. Find the value of r.
questions.explanation: > Cell efficiency = R/(R+r), so 0.75 = 6/(6+r), giving 6+r = 8, so r = 2.0Ω. The efficiency formula directly compares the useful external resistance to the total circuit resistance, meaning a higher internal resistance always lowers the fraction of power delivered usefully — this trade-off between r and efficiency is a frequently recurring JAMB theme.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Nuclear Fusion] The process of energy production in the sun is
questions.explanation: > The Sun generates energy through nuclear fusion, where hydrogen nuclei combine under immense heat and pressure to form helium, releasing vast amounts of energy per the mass-energy equivalence relation. Nuclear fission (splitting heavy nuclei, option A) is the process used in nuclear power plants on Earth, not what powers stars — this fission/fusion mix-up is one of the most commonly tested distractor traps in nuclear physics.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Current Electricity — Terminal Voltage and Internal Resistance] A resistance R is connected across the terminal of an electric cell of internal resistance 2Ω and the voltage was reduced to 3/5 of its nominal value. The value of R is
questions.explanation: > Terminal voltage V relates to e.m.f. ε by V/ε = R/(R+r). Setting V/ε = 3/5 and r = 2Ω: R/(R+2) = 3/5, so 5R = 3R + 6, giving 2R = 6, R = 3Ω. This models how a cell's terminal voltage always drops below its rated e.m.f. once current flows through any external resistance, due to the "lost volts" across the internal resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Transformers]
options: power line. If the secondary coil has 1,000 turns and a terminal voltage of 1,200 volts, what is the value of N?
questions.explanation: > The transformer turns ratio equation states Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, so Np = Ns × (Vp/Vs) = 1000 × (120/1200) = 100. Since the secondary voltage (1200V) is higher than the primary (120V), this is confirmed as a step-up transformer, meaning the secondary must have more turns than the primary, consistent with 1000 turns on the secondary versus only 100 on the primary.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Variation of Weight on Earth's Surface] I. The earth is not spherical but elliptical in shape II. Variation in latitude and longitude III. Rotation of the earth on its axis IV. Variation in the density of the earth On which combination of the above does the weight of an object vary on the earth's surface?
questions.explanation: > Weight (mg) varies across Earth's surface because Earth's slightly ellipsoidal shape (I) means the radius — and hence g — differs by latitude, and Earth's rotation (III) creates a centrifugal effect that reduces effective weight, strongest at the equator and zero at the poles. Longitude (part of II, alongside latitude) has no bearing on g since g depends on distance from Earth's centre and rotational effects, not east-west position — but since latitude variation alone is a genuine cause, and IV (density variation, a purely local/geological effect not part of the standard three global causes) is excluded, I, II and III together form the examiner's intended answer.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Conservation of Energy] A stone of mass 1kg is dropped from a height of 10m above the ground and falls freely under gravity. Its kinetic energy 5m above the ground is then equal to
options: its kinetic energy on the ground
questions.explanation: > By conservation of mechanical energy, total energy (KE + PE) remains constant throughout the fall. At the halfway point (5m), exactly half of the initial potential energy has converted to kinetic energy, while the other half remains as potential energy — so KE at 5m = ½(initial PE). This halfway-point symmetry is a hallmark feature of free-fall energy conversion problems.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Harmonics on a Stretched String] Find the frequencies of the first three harmonics of a piano string of length 1.5m, if the velocity of the wave on the string is 120ms⁻¹
questions.explanation: > The fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends is f₁ = v/(2L) = 120/(2×1.5) = 40Hz. Successive harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental: f₂ = 2×40 = 80Hz, and f₃ = 3×40 = 120Hz. This whole-number multiple pattern (f, 2f, 3f...) is the defining signature of harmonics on a string fixed at both ends, distinct from the odd-harmonic-only pattern seen in pipes closed at one end.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Standing Waves in Sound / Antinodes] A plane sound wave of frequency 85.5Hz and velocity 342ms⁻¹ is reflected from a vertical wall. At what distance from the wall does the wave have antinode?
questions.explanation: > Wavelength λ = v/f = 342/85.5 = 4m. When a sound wave reflects off a rigid wall, a node (point of zero displacement) forms at the wall itself, and the nearest antinode forms at a quarter-wavelength away: d = λ/4 = 4/4 = 1m. This node-at-the-boundary condition mirrors how a closed pipe end behaves for standing sound waves.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electrostatics/Gravitation — Comparing Fundamental Forces] The ratio of electrostatic force F_E to gravitational force F_G between two protons each of charge e and mass m, at a distance d is
questions.explanation: > Coulomb's law gives F_E = e²/(4πε₀d²) and Newton's law of gravitation gives F_G = Gm²/d², so their ratio F_E/F_G = e²/(4πε₀Gm²) — note the distance d cancels out entirely from the ratio, which is why none of the options contain d. This ratio famously comes out enormous (~10³⁶), illustrating just how much stronger the electrostatic force is than gravity at the subatomic scale.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Electric Field Strength] A student is at a height 4m above the ground during a thunderstorm. Given that the potential difference between the thundercloud and the ground is 10⁷V, the electric field created by the storm is
questions.explanation: > Electric field strength between parallel-like surfaces is E = V/d = 10⁷/4 = 2.5×10⁶ NC⁻¹. This treats the cloud-to-ground gap as a simple parallel-plate-like field, a standard simplification for estimating storm field strengths in introductory physics. The trap is using the student's height in the wrong place or forgetting to divide, both of which lead to a mismatched power of ten.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Angle of Dip] What is the angle of dip at the magnetic equator?
questions.explanation: > The angle of dip is the angle Earth's magnetic field lines make with the horizontal at a given location. At the magnetic equator, the field lines run parallel to Earth's surface (purely horizontal, with no vertical component), giving a dip angle of exactly 0°. The dip increases progressively toward the magnetic poles, reaching a maximum of 90° (field pointing straight down/up) at the poles themselves.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Radiation Shielding] Which of the following metals will provide the greatest shield against ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: > Lead is the standard shielding material against ionising radiation (especially gamma rays and X-rays) because of its very high density and high atomic number, which maximise the probability of photon absorption/interaction per unit thickness. Aluminium, by contrast, is commonly used only to block much less penetrating alpha and some beta particles, not the more penetrating radiation types this question implies.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electrochemistry — Voltaic Cells] In a Daniel cell, the depolarizer, positive and negative electrodes are respectively
options: sulphuric acid, lead oxide and lead
questions.explanation: > In a Daniell cell, copper sulphate solution acts as the depolarizer (preventing hydrogen gas bubbles from forming at the copper electrode, which would otherwise cause polarization and reduce current), with copper as the positive electrode and zinc as the negative electrode. The other options describe entirely different cell types: manganese dioxide/carbon/zinc is a dry (Leclanché) cell, while sulphuric acid/lead oxide/lead is a lead-acid accumulator.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor] The force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field is greatest when the
options: conductor makes an angle of 60° with the field
force is independent of the angles between the fields and the conductor
conductor is parallel with the field
conductor is at right angle with the field
questions.explanation: > The force on a current-carrying conductor is F = BIL sinθ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. This is maximised when sinθ = 1, i.e., θ = 90° (conductor perpendicular to the field). When the conductor is parallel to the field (θ = 0°), sinθ = 0 and the force drops to zero entirely — this is why motors and generators are designed with coils oriented to maximise this perpendicular geometry.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Rotation of Reflected Rays] A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. If the mirror is rotated through 10°, through what angle is the reflected ray rotated?
questions.explanation: > A key optical law states that when a plane mirror is rotated through an angle θ (with the incident ray fixed), the reflected ray rotates through 2θ — twice the mirror's rotation — regardless of the original angle of incidence. Here, rotating the mirror by 10° rotates the reflected ray by 2×10° = 20°. The original 35° incidence angle is a distractor; it plays no role in this particular calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — AC Circuits / Resonance]
questions.explanation: > At resonance in a series RLC circuit, the inductive and capacitive reactances exactly cancel (X_L = X_C), leaving only resistance to oppose the current. This means voltage and current are perfectly in phase, giving a phase angle of 0°. This in-phase condition is precisely what makes resonance the point of maximum current flow in a series RLC circuit.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Power and Efficiency of Motors] A working electric motor takes a current of 1.5 A when the p.d across it is 250V. If its efficiency is 80%, the power output is
questions.explanation: > Power input to the motor is P = VI = 250 × 1.5 = 375W. Power output = efficiency × power input = 0.8 × 375 = 300W. The remaining 75W (375 − 300) is lost as heat and friction within the motor itself, which is exactly what "efficiency less than 100%" always represents for real machines and motors.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — RMS Values in AC Circuits]
options: c circuit is given as 2 sin wt. Determine the
questions.explanation: > The "d.c. equivalent" of an AC current refers to its RMS (root-mean-square) value, which for a sinusoidal current i = I₀sin(ωt) is I_rms = I₀/√2. Here I₀ = 2A, so I_rms = 2/√2 = √2 A. The RMS value is defined precisely because it's the DC current that would dissipate the same average power in a resistor as the actual AC current does.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — LC Resonance] A capacitor of 20 x 10⁻¹²F and an inductor are joined in series. The value of the inductance that will give the circuit a resonance frequency of 200 kHz is
questions.explanation: > Resonance frequency for an LC circuit is f = 1/(2π√(LC)), so L = 1/((2πf)²C). Substituting f = 200×10³Hz and C = 20×10⁻¹²F gives L ≈ 0.0317H, which is closest to 1/32 H (≈0.03125H) among the given options. This LC resonance relationship is the basis for tuning circuits in radios, where L or C is adjusted to select a desired station's frequency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Gas Laws / Combined Gas Law] The pressure of a given mass of a gas changes from 300Nm⁻² to 120Nm⁻² while the temperature drops from 127°C to −73°C. The ratio of the final volume to the initial volume is
questions.explanation: > Using the combined gas law (P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂) with temperatures converted to Kelvin (T₁ = 127+273 = 400K, T₂ = −73+273 = 200K): V₂/V₁ = (P₁T₂)/(P₂T₁) = (300×200)/(120×400) = 60000/48000 = 1.25 = 5/4. The critical step many students skip is converting Celsius to Kelvin before substituting — gas law ratios only work correctly with absolute temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Simple Machines / Efficiency] The efficiency of a machine is always less than 100% because the
options: work output is always greater than the work input
load lifted is always greater than the effort applied
effort applied is always greater than the load lifted
velocity ratio is always greater than the mechanical advantage
questions.explanation: > Efficiency = (Mechanical Advantage/Velocity Ratio) × 100%, and since real machines always lose some energy to friction and other resistances, the mechanical advantage (actual load/effort ratio achieved) is always somewhat less than the ideal velocity ratio (the ratio determined purely by the machine's geometry). This gap — VR always exceeding MA — is precisely why no real machine can reach 100% efficiency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Current Electricity — Internal Resistance from Two Readings] A cell can supply current of 0.4 A and 0.2 A through a 4.0Ω and 10.0Ω resistor respectively. This internal resistance of the cell is
questions.explanation: > Since the same cell's e.m.f. must equal I(R+r) in both cases: 0.4(4+r) = 0.2(10+r). Expanding: 1.6 + 0.4r = 2 + 0.2r, so 0.2r = 0.4, giving r = 2.0Ω. This technique — setting two expressions for the same e.m.f. equal to each other — is the standard method whenever a cell's internal resistance must be found from two different external resistor readings rather than from a single circuit.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Speed of Sound] I. Temperature. II. Density of air molecules III. Pressure IV. Pitch Which of the above will affect the velocity of sound in the air
questions.explanation: > The speed of sound in air depends on temperature (higher temperature means faster molecular motion, so faster sound propagation) and on the density/elastic properties of the medium (II). Pressure (III) has essentially no direct effect at constant temperature, since increasing pressure raises density proportionally in a way that cancels out in the speed formula. Pitch (IV) is a property of the sound wave itself (related to frequency), not a property of the air that could influence how fast any sound travels through it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Simple Machines / Wheel and Axle] A wheel and axle is used to raise a load of 500 N by the application of an effort of 250 N. If the radii of the wheel and the axle are 0.4 cm and 0.1 cm respectively, the efficiency of the machine is
questions.explanation: > For a wheel and axle, velocity ratio = R_wheel/R_axle = 0.4/0.1 = 4. Mechanical advantage = Load/Effort = 500/250 = 2. Efficiency = (MA/VR) × 100% = (2/4) × 100% = 50%. The gap between MA and VR here represents the energy lost to friction in the machine's bearings, which is why no real wheel-and-axle system reaches the full velocity ratio as its mechanical advantage.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Friction and Work Done] A bead travelling on a straight line wire is brought to rest at 0.2m by friction. If the mass of the bead is 0.01kg and the coefficient of friction between the bead and the wire is 0.1, determine the work done by the friction [g = 10ms⁻²]
questions.explanation: > Frictional force = μmg = 0.1 × 0.01 × 10 = 0.01N. Work done by friction = force × distance = 0.01 × 0.2 = 0.002J = 2×10⁻³J. Since friction always opposes motion, this work done "by" friction is technically negative (removing kinetic energy from the bead), but the magnitude asked for here is 2×10⁻³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Gravitation — Newton's Law of Gravitation] If the distance between two suspended masses 10kg each is tripled, the gravitational force of attraction between them is reduced by
questions.explanation: > Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law: F ∝ 1/d². Tripling the distance means the new force is F/3² = F/9, so the force is reduced to one-ninth of its original value. This inverse-square relationship is shared by gravitational, electrostatic, and several other fundamental force laws, making "distance tripled → force to one-ninth" a frequently recurring calculation pattern across physics topics.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Polarization] Vibration in a stretched spring cannot be polarized because they are
questions.explanation: > Polarization is a phenomenon exclusive to transverse waves, where oscillations occur only in one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel — a polarizing filter can then selectively block certain orientations. Vibrations along a stretched spring (compressions and rarefactions travelling along its length) are longitudinal waves, oscillating parallel to the direction of propagation, which have no transverse plane to restrict, and therefore cannot be polarized at all.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Radioactive Decay / Half-life] The percentage of the original nuclei of the sample of a radioactive substance left after 5 half-lives is
questions.explanation: > After n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ. After 5 half-lives: (1/2)⁵ = 1/32 ≈ 0.03125, which as a percentage is approximately 3.1%, closest to option C. A common trap is confusing "5 half-lives" with simply dividing by 5, which would incorrectly give 20% remaining instead of the correct exponential decay result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Stationary Waves] Which of the following is a characteristic of stationary waves?
options: They are formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
they can be transverse or longitudinal
The distance between two successive nodes is one wavelength
The antinode is a point of minimum displacement
questions.explanation: > Stationary (standing) waves form specifically from the superposition of two identical waves (same amplitude, frequency, and wavelength) travelling in opposite directions, typically from a wave and its reflection. Option C is false since the distance between successive nodes is actually half a wavelength, not a full wavelength, and option D reverses the definitions — the antinode is a point of *maximum*, not minimum, displacement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Biology of Vision / Optics — The Eye] The eye controls the amount of light reaching the retina by adjusting the
questions.explanation: > The iris is the coloured, muscular part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil opening, dilating in dim light to let more light in and constricting in bright light to protect the retina from overexposure. The cornea and retina are fixed structures with other roles (initial focusing and light detection respectively), while the optic nerve simply transmits the resulting signal to the brain and plays no role in regulating light intake.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Nuclear Reactions] ²³₁₁Na + X → ²⁰₉F + ⁴₂He What particle is X in the reaction above?
questions.explanation: > Balancing mass numbers: 23 + A_X = 20 + 4, giving A_X = 1. Balancing atomic numbers: 11 + Z_X = 9 + 2, giving Z_X = 0. A particle with mass number 1 and atomic number 0 is a neutron, meaning this is a neutron-capture reaction. Alpha particles (A=4, Z=2), beta particles (A≈0, Z=−1), and gamma rays (A=0, Z=0 but massless/chargeless radiation, not a nucleon) all fail to satisfy this specific mass-and-charge balance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Resultant of Perpendicular Forces] Two forces each of 10N act on a body, one towards the north and the other towards the east. The magnitude and the direction of the resultant force are
questions.explanation: > Since the two 10N forces are perpendicular (north and east), the resultant magnitude is found via Pythagoras: R = √(10² + 10²) = 10√2N ≈ 14.1N. Because the forces are equal in magnitude, the resultant bisects the angle between north and east exactly, giving a direction of N45°E (45° east of north), ruling out the westward options which point in entirely the wrong general direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Circular Motion / Angular Velocity] A particle in circular motion performs 30 oscillations in 6 seconds. Its angular velocity is
questions.explanation: > Frequency of oscillation f = 30/6 = 5Hz. Angular velocity ω = 2πf = 2π(5) = 10π rad/s. The factor of 2π is essential here — forgetting it and just reporting frequency directly (5 rad/s) is the most common error, confusing frequency in Hz with angular velocity in rad/s, which differ by exactly this factor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Power Transmission] From the generating station to each substation power is transmitted at a very high voltage so as to reduce
questions.explanation: > Transmitting power at high voltage keeps the current low for a given power (since P = VI), and since resistive heating loss is I²R, a lower current dramatically reduces power dissipated as heat in the transmission cables. Hysteresis and eddy current losses (options A and B) are specifically transformer/magnetic-core phenomena, not properties of the transmission cables themselves, so raising transmission voltage does not target those losses.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Concave Mirrors and Magnification] A concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm forms a real image twice as large as the object. The object distance is
questions.explanation: > Focal length f = R/2 = 20cm. For a real, inverted image magnified 2×, magnification m = −v/u = −2, so v = 2u. Substituting into the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f: 1/(2u) + 1/u = 1/20, giving 3/(2u) = 1/20, so u = 30cm. This places the object between the focus (20cm) and the centre of curvature (40cm), exactly where concave mirrors are known to produce magnified, real, inverted images.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Apparent Displacement Through a Glass Block] A coin placed below a rectangular glass block of thickness 9cm and refractive index 1.5 is viewed vertically above the block. The apparent displacement of the coin is
questions.explanation: > Apparent displacement (how much closer the coin appears to be) is given by t(1 − 1/n), where t is the block's thickness and n is the refractive index. Substituting: 9 × (1 − 1/1.5) = 9 × (1/3) = 3cm. This formula is closely related to the apparent-depth calculation, but specifically measures the shift caused by the refracting slab rather than the apparent depth itself.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electrochemistry — Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis] A current of 0.5 A flowing 3h deposits 2g of metal during electrolysis. The quantity of the same metal that would be deposited by a current of 1.5A flowing for 1h is
questions.explanation: > Mass deposited is proportional to total charge passed, Q = It. First scenario: Q₁ = 0.5A × 3h = 1.5 A·h. Second scenario: Q₂ = 1.5A × 1h = 1.5 A·h. Since the total charge is identical in both cases, the mass deposited must also be identical: 2g. This is a classic "same charge, different current/time combination" trap designed to test whether students genuinely understand Faraday's law depends on the product It, not on current or time individually.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Thermometric Liquids] Water is a poor thermometric liquid because it
questions.explanation: > Water "wets" glass, meaning it clings to and spreads along the inner surface of a glass thermometer tube rather than moving cleanly as a single column, which makes readings inconsistent and imprecise. Mercury, by contrast, does not wet glass and moves as a clean, well-defined column, which is why it (despite its toxicity concerns) has traditionally been preferred as a thermometric liquid over water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Evaporation] Blowing air over a liquid aids evaporation by
questions.explanation: > Blowing air over a liquid's surface continuously sweeps away the vapour molecules that have already evaporated, keeping the local vapour pressure just above the liquid low and preventing saturation. This maintains a steep concentration gradient that keeps driving more molecules to evaporate — precisely the same principle behind why laundry on a windy day dries faster than on a still day, without any actual temperature increase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Current Electricity — Terminal Voltage and Internal Resistance] An electric cell with nominal voltage E has a resistance of 3Ω connected across it. If the voltage falls to 0.6E, the internal resistance of the cell is
questions.explanation: > Terminal voltage relates to e.m.f. by V/E = R/(R+r). Setting V/E = 0.6 and R = 3Ω: 3/(3+r) = 0.6, so 3 = 0.6(3+r) = 1.8 + 0.6r, giving 0.6r = 1.2, so r = 2Ω. The greater the voltage drop from the nominal e.m.f., the larger the internal resistance relative to the external load — this proportional relationship is the basis for measuring a cell's "health" via its internal resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetic Spectrum — Infrared Radiation] The electromagnetic wave that can produce a heating effect on the environment is
questions.explanation: > Infrared radiation is specifically associated with heat, since it's readily absorbed by matter and increases molecular vibration, which is experienced as a temperature rise — this is the principle behind infrared heaters and why we feel warmth from sunlight even without visible light present. X-rays, gamma rays, and UV are all higher-energy, shorter-wavelength radiation associated primarily with ionisation effects on matter rather than bulk heating.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Fluids — Hydrostatic Pressure] The hydrostatic blood pressure difference between the head and the feet of a boy standing straight is 1.65 x 10⁴ Nm⁻². Find the height of the boy. [Density of blood = 1.1 x 10³ kgm⁻³, g = 10ms⁻²]
questions.explanation: > Hydrostatic pressure difference is P = ρgh, so h = P/(ρg) = (1.65×10⁴)/(1.1×10³ × 10) = 16500/11000 = 1.5m. This is a direct real-world application of the same pressure-depth formula used for fluids in tanks or oceans, here applied to the column of blood in the human circulatory system.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Modern Physics — Nuclear Fission] The particle that is responsible for the nuclear fission in a nuclear reactor is
questions.explanation: > Nuclear fission in a reactor is triggered when a free neutron strikes a heavy, fissile nucleus (like Uranium-235), causing it to split and release energy along with additional neutrons that sustain a chain reaction. Neutrons are used specifically because they carry no charge, so they aren't repelled by the positively charged nucleus, unlike protons which would be strongly deflected by electrostatic repulsion before ever reaching it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Mechanics — Newton's Second Law / Apparent Weight in a Lift] A body weighing 80N stands in an elevator that is about to move. The force exerted by the floor on the body as the elevator moves upward with an acceleration of 5 ms⁻² is [g = 10ms⁻²]
questions.explanation: > Mass of the body = W/g = 80/10 = 8kg. When the elevator accelerates upward, the normal force N from the floor must supply both the body's weight and the extra force needed for upward acceleration: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g+a) = 8 × (10+5) = 120N. This is the same physics behind feeling heavier when an elevator starts moving up and lighter when it starts moving down — the normal force (what a scale would read) always shifts with the elevator's acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Optics — Refraction at Normal Incidence] A ray of light which strikes a glass slab from air at normal incidence passes through the slab
options: undeviated and undisplaced at a lower speed
deviated and undisplaced at a lower speed
deviated and displaced at a lower speed
undeviated and displaced at a faster speed
questions.explanation: > At normal incidence (0° angle of incidence, striking the surface perpendicular), there is no bending of the ray at all, so it travels straight through without any deviation or lateral displacement. However, the ray's speed does slow down inside the denser glass medium (v = c/n), since refractive index always affects propagation speed regardless of the angle of entry.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Fluids — Archimedes' Principle / Upthrust Ratios] A copper cube weighs 0.25 N in air, 0.17N when completely immersed in paraffin oil and 0.15 N when completely immersed in water. The ratio of upthrust in oil to upthrust in water is
questions.explanation: > Upthrust equals the apparent loss of weight: in oil, upthrust = 0.25 − 0.17 = 0.08N; in water, upthrust = 0.25 − 0.15 = 0.10N. The ratio is 0.08:0.10, which simplifies to 4:5. Since the cube's volume is identical in both liquids, this ratio directly reflects the ratio of the two liquids' densities (oil being less dense than water).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Fuse Ratings] When connected to a mains of 250V, the fuse rating in the plug of an electric device of 1 KW is
questions.explanation: > Current drawn by the device is I = P/V = 1000/250 = 4A. A fuse must be rated at or slightly above the normal operating current to avoid nuisance blowing while still protecting against genuine overloads, so the fuse rating here corresponds directly to this calculated 4A operating current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Capacitive Reactance] At what frequency would a capacitor of 2.5μF used in a radio circuit have a reactance of 250Ω
questions.explanation: > Capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC), so f = 1/(2πX_CC) = 1/(2π × 250 × 2.5×10⁻⁶) = 800/π Hz ≈ 254.6Hz. This inverse relationship means capacitive reactance drops as frequency rises — the opposite behaviour to inductive reactance — which is exactly why capacitors and inductors are paired in radio tuning circuits to select a specific resonant frequency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Wave Speed on a String from Fundamental Frequency] If tension is maintained on a stretched string of length 0.6m, such that its fundamental frequency of 220Hz is excited, determine the velocity of the transverse wave in the string.
questions.explanation: > For a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental wavelength is twice the string's length: λ = 2L = 2(0.6) = 1.2m. Wave velocity v = fλ = 220 × 1.2 = 264 m/s. This relationship (fundamental wavelength = 2L) is the foundation for tuning stringed instruments, where adjusting tension changes wave velocity and hence the fundamental pitch produced.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Thermal Physics — Heat Transfer in Engines] The radiator of a motor car is cooled by
questions.explanation: > A car radiator relies on airflow (either from the vehicle's motion or a fan) passing over its fins to carry away heat, which is a convection process — the moving air continuously replaces warmed air near the radiator surface with cooler air. While the metal fins do conduct heat from the coolant to their outer surface, the dominant mechanism for actually removing that heat into the surrounding environment is convection via the airflow.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electromagnetism — Moving Coil Galvanometer] Which of the following statements is true of the properties of a moving coil galvanometer?
options: The coil has a small area
There are strong hair springs to give a large control panel
There is a strong permanent magnet to give high magnetic flux
it has a small number of turns of coil
questions.explanation: > A sensitive moving coil galvanometer is designed with a strong permanent magnet to produce a high magnetic flux density, which maximises the deflecting torque (proportional to BANI) on the coil for even small currents. In contrast, sensitive galvanometers actually use a large coil area and many turns (not few, ruling out A and D) to further boost this torque, and use weak (not strong) control springs so that even tiny currents produce a noticeable, easily-readable deflection.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Electricity — Power and Resistance] An electric iron is rated 1000W, 230V. What is the resistance of its elements?
questions.explanation: > Using P = V²/R, resistance R = V²/P = 230²/1000 = 52900/1000 = 52.9Ω. This power-voltage-resistance relationship (P=V²/R) is the most direct route whenever a device's power rating and operating voltage are both given but current is not — no need to first compute current separately.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: [Waves — Properties of Travelling Waves] The property that is propagated in a travelling wave is
questions.explanation: > A travelling wave transports energy from one point to another through the medium, without the medium's particles themselves undergoing any net displacement — each particle simply oscillates about its equilibrium position and passes the disturbance (and its energy) to the next. Frequency, amplitude, and wavelength are all fixed characteristic properties describing the wave's behaviour, not something that itself moves or is "propagated" from source to observer.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Which of these colours in the visible spectrum has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency in the visible spectrum, while violet has the shortest.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A man moves 6.0m East and then 10.0m N30ºE. How far is he from his starting point?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Structure of matter and kinetic theory
questions.question: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls equals.
options: Momentum imparted to the walls per unit area.
Change in momentum per unit volume.
Change in momentum imparted to the walls per unit area.
Rate of change of momentum imparted to the walls per second per unit area.
questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area, and force is the rate of change of momentum. Thus, pressure = rate of momentum change per unit area.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Which of the following is not true about a wave in a plucked string?
questions.explanation: Plucked string waves are mechanical and transverse, with crests and troughs; they are not longitudinal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The emf of a cell is the potential difference across its terminals when it is in
questions.explanation: EMF is the terminal voltage when no current flows (open circuit). It is the maximum voltage the cell can provide.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The thermometric property of mercury is best on the change in
questions.explanation: Mercury thermometers rely on the volume expansion of mercury with temperature, which is relatively uniform.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Some of the features of the human eye that greatly help to refract light entering the eyes are
questions.explanation: The cornea does most of the refraction, and the lens fine-tunes focusing; both are the main refracting structures.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: When both the object and its image move together in the same direction relative to the observer, then there is
questions.explanation: If the object and image move together, they occupy the same position, eliminating the apparent shift seen in parallax.
